Shift Reduce Parsers and Its Conflicts
• The general shift-reduce technique is: 
 
– if there is no handle on the stack then shift 
 
– If there is a handle then reduce 
• Bottom-up parsing is essentially the process of detecting handles and reducing them. 
• Different bottom-up parsers differ in the way they detect handles. 
• Conflicts
•
What happens when there is a choice 
 
–What action to take in case both shift and reduce are valid? shift-reduce conflict 
 
–Which rule to use for reduction if reduction is possible by more than one rule? reduce-reduce 
conflict 
59

pages.source_path: data\raw\college\5. Bottom Up Parser Compiler Design-58-86 (1).pdf
pages.text:
Conflicts 
Shift-Reduce Conflict: parser is unsure whether it should: (1) Shift (read the next input 
symbol), or (2) Reduce (apply a grammar rule).
Left Table Explanation “(Reduce First)”
Wrong Prediction Bcz + before *
Right Table Explanation “(Shift First)”: 
Valid Bcz * first before +
60

pages.source_path: data\raw\college\5. Bottom Up Parser Compiler Design-58-86 (1).pdf
pages.text:
Conflicts
Reduce-reduce conflict: happens when the parser finds more than one rule that can 
be applied to reduce the same substring.
Left Table Explanation 
(Reduce by R → c first, then M → R+R)
Right Table Explanation:
(Reduce by M → R+c directly)
•
Left Table Path: parses c+c as M → R+R
•
Right Table Path: parses c+c as M → R+c
•
Both valid → this is why it’s called a 
Reduce-Reduce Conflict.
61

Shift-Reduce Parsers
•
There are two main categories of shift-reduce parsers
1. Operator-Precedence Parser
• simple, but only a small class of grammars.
2. LR-Parsers
• covers wide range of grammars.
• SLR – simple LR parser 
• Canonical LR – most general LR parser
• LALR – intermediate LR parser (look-head LR parser)
• SLR, CLR and LALR work same, only their parsing tables are different.

• The most powerful shift-reduce parsing is:
  
 
 LR(k) parsing.
  
left to right

(k is omitted ➔ it is 1)
• LR parsing is attractive because:
• LR parsing is most general non-backtracking shift-reduce parsing, yet it is efficient.
• Every LL(1) grammar is automatically an LR(1) grammar, but there are many LR(1) grammars that cannot 
be parsed using LL(1) rules. 
 
LL(1)-Grammars   LR(1)-Grammars
• An LR-parser can detect a syntactic error as soon as it is possible to do so a left-to-right scan of the 
input.

LR parsing Algorithm in pseudocode
Input pointer (ip) points to the first symbol of w i/p string.
At each step, look at current state (S) and input symbol (a) 
from the input pointer. There are 4 possible actions:
Case 1: Shift
Case 2: Reduce
Case 3: Accept
Parsing succeeds → Exit
Case 4: Error
Report syntax error → Exit parsing.

Production to Use for Reduction (Readings)
• How do we know which production to apply in a given configuration 
• We can guess! – May require backtracking 
• Keep track of “ALL” possible rules that can apply at a given point in the input 
string 
77

pages.source_path: data\raw\college\5. Bottom Up Parser Compiler Design-58-86 (1).pdf
pages.text:
Parser states (Readings) 
• Goal is to know the valid reductions at any given point 
• Summarize all possible stack prefixes α as a parser state 
• Parser state is defined by a DFA state that reads in the stack α 
• Accept states of DFA are unique reductions
78

pages.source_path: data\raw\college\5. Bottom Up Parser Compiler Design-58-86 (1).pdf
pages.text:
Viable prefixes (Readings)
• α is a viable prefix of the grammar if 
 
– ∃w such that αw is a right sentential form 
 
– is a configuration of the parser 
• As long as the parser has viable prefixes on the stack no parser error 
has been seen 
• The set of viable prefixes is a regular language 
• We can construct an automaton that accepts viable prefixes
79

pages.text:
Constructing Parse Table
 
 
Augment the grammar 
• G is a grammar with start symbol S 
• The augmented grammar G’ for G has a new start symbol S’ and an 
additional production S’ → S 
• When the parser reduces by this rule it will stop with accept
80

pages.source_path: data\raw\college\5. Bottom Up Parser Compiler Design-58-86 (1).pdf
pages.text:
LR(0) items 
• An LR(0) item of a grammar G is a production of G with a special symbol “.” at 
some position of the right side.
• Thus, production A→XYZ gives four LR(0) items
•
An item indicates how much of a production has been seen 
at a point in the process of parsing 
– Symbols on the left of “.” are already on the stacks 
– Symbols on the right of “.” are expected in the input
81

pages.source_path: data\raw\college\5. Bottom Up Parser Compiler Design-58-86 (1).pdf
pages.text:
Start state
• Start state of DFA is an empty stack corresponding to S’ →.S item 
• This means no input has been seen 
• The parser expects to see a string derived from S
•
Closure of a state adds items for all productions whose LHS occurs in an item in the state, just after 
“.” 
 
– Set of possible productions to be reduced next 
 
– Added items have “.” located at the beginning 
 
– No symbol of these items is on the stack as yet 
82

pages.source_path: data\raw\college\5. Bottom Up Parser Compiler Design-58-86 (1).pdf
pages.text:
Closure operation
• Let I be a set of items for a grammar G 
• closure(I) is a set constructed as follows: 
 
– Every item in I is in closure (I) 
 
– If A → α.Bβ is in closure(I) and B → γ is a production then B → .γ is in closure(I) 
• Naturally A → α.Bβ indicates that we expect a string derivable from Bβ in input 
• If B → γ is a production then we might see a string derivable from γ at this point
83
